To test this hypothesis, we predict that overexpression of AKR1B1 in breast cancer cell lines will increase ROS levels, resulting in greater DNA damage and cell proliferation compared to control cells. Conversely, knocking down AKR1B1 should reduce ROS levels and decrease both DNA damage and cancer cell proliferation. Confirmation of this hypothesis would involve measuring increased ROS and DNA damage markers upon AKR1B1 overexpression, and reduction of these markers following its knockdown.

We hypothesize that the enzyme NDUFB1, a subunit of Complex I in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, affects levels of glyoxylate, a precursor in oxalate biosynthesis, thus influencing Hyperoxaluria primary 1 (PH1) pathogenesis. In PH1, defective alanine-glyoxylate aminotransferase leads to glyoxylate buildup, increasing oxalate production. NDUFB1 dysfunction may impair mitochondrial oxidative phosphorylation, altering NAD+/NADH ratios. This shift could suppress lactate dehydrogenase activity, which in atypical conditions converts pyruvate to lactate while preventing excessive glyoxylate buildup. Lower lactate production would indirectly elevate glyoxylate levels, exacerbating oxalate formation and stone formation in PH1. We predict that inhibiting NDUFB1 in a cellular model of PH1 will elevate oxalate beyond that seen with PH1 mutations alone, indicating exacerbation through altered NAD+/NADH ratios. Conversely, restoring NDUFB1 function should normalize oxalate levels. Detection of increased oxalate with NDUFB1 inhibition would confirm the hypothesis, while no change would refute it.

We hypothesize that the enzyme 3-hydroxyacyl-CoA dehydratase 2 (HTD2) contributes to Mitochondrial DNA depletion syndrome 21 (MTDPS21) through impaired fatty acid β-oxidation, leading to decreased availability of acetyl-CoA. This acetyl-CoA shortfall may hinder the TCA cycle, reducing NADH/FADH2 production and compromising the mitochondrial electron transport chain. Consequently, this results in attenuated ATP synthesis and insufficient maintenance of mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA), causing its depletion. 

A specific, falsifiable prediction is that silencing HTD2 expression in a cellular model will lead to decreased acetyl-CoA and ATP levels, followed by reduced mtDNA content. Conversely, overexpressing HTD2 should restore normal acetyl-CoA, ATP, and mtDNA levels. This hypothesis is grounded in the biochemical fact that HTD2 is crucial for fatty acid degradation, linking its dysfunction to energy and nucleic acid imbalances characteristic of MTDPS21.

We hypothesize that ELOVL6, an enzyme involved in elongating fatty acids, influences retinal development, leading to Microphthalmia, isolated, 8 by altering lipid composition critical for eye development. Specifically, ELOVL6 elongates long-chain fatty acids to very-long-chain fatty acids (VLCFAs), which are integral to retinal cell membrane structure and function. Aberrant function or expression of ELOVL6 could disrupt VLCFA homeostasis, impairing photoreceptor cell development and survival, resulting in microphthalmia. 

To test this hypothesis, we propose generating a conditional knockout of ELOVL6 in retinal progenitor cells in a mouse model. We predict that ELOVL6 deletion will lead to reduced VLCFAs in the retina and smaller eye size, recapitulating microphthalmia phenotypes. Detection of normal VLCFA levels and eye development in wild-type mice or corrected VLCFA levels and phenotype rescue in knockout rescue experiments would support or refute this hypothesis, respectively.

We hypothesize that ACER3 (alkaline ceramidase 3) contributes to uncombable hair syndrome 2 through dysregulation of ceramide metabolism, affecting hair follicle structure. ACER3 is responsible for hydrolyzing ceramides into sphingosine, a lipid involved in cell signaling. We propose that a deficiency or malfunction of ACER3 leads to abnormal ceramide accumulation in hair follicles, disrupting lipid composition and keratinocyte differentiation. This imbalance alters the physical properties and structural integrity of the hair shaft, resulting in unruly and uncombable hair characteristics. To confirm this hypothesis, we predict that ACER3-deficient models will exhibit increased ceramide levels and disorganized hair follicle architecture. Conversely, restoring ACER3 activity should normalize ceramide levels and improve hair morphology. These outcomes can be assessed through lipidomics and histological hair follicle analysis. Refutation would involve no change in ceramide levels or hair structure upon manipulation of ACER3 activity.

We hypothesize that phosphopantothenoylcysteine synthetase (PPCS) modulates the pathophysiology of Transaldolase deficiency via disruption of the pentose phosphate pathway (PPP). In Transaldolase deficiency, impaired transaldolase activity leads to accumulation of sedoheptulose-7-phosphate and decreased ribose-5-phosphate. PPCS, involved in Coenzyme A biosynthesis, may exacerbate these metabolic imbalances by limiting Coenzyme A availability, thus impairing acetyl-CoA production critical for the synthesis of ribose-5-phosphate derivatives. We predict that overexpressing PPCS in cells with transaldolase knockdown will decrease sedoheptulose-7-phosphate accumulation and restore ribose-5-phosphate levels, observable via targeted metabolomic analysis. Conversely, PPCS inhibition should worsen metabolite imbalances, further confirming the pathway involvement. These predictions, if confirmed, would elucidate a novel metabolic link between PPCS activity and PPP dysfunction in Transaldolase deficiency, enhancing our understanding of the disease mechanism.

We hypothesize that serine racemase (SRR) contributes to hypophosphatemic rickets, autosomal recessive, 2, through dysregulation of D-serine production, which affects phosphate metabolism. SRR catalyzes the interconversion of L-serine to D-serine, a co-agonist at NMDA-type glutamate receptors. Altered SRR function could disrupt neuronal signaling, modulating factors like FGF23 and PHEX, crucial in phosphate regulation. This dysregulation may lead to impaired renal phosphate reabsorption and bone mineralization, characteristic of the disease. A specific, falsifiable prediction is that knockout or inhibition of SRR in a murine model mimics the hypophosphatemic phenotype with elevated urinary phosphate levels and altered FGF23 expression. Conversely, normal phosphate levels and unaltered FGF23 in SRR-deficient models would refute this hypothesis. This implicates SRR as a novel modulator of phosphate homeostasis, linking neuronal activity to metabolic bone disease.

We hypothesize that the enzyme methionine synthase (MTR) impacts coenzyme Q10 deficiency, primary, 2 through altered methylation of genes involved in CoQ10 biosynthesis. MTR catalyzes the remethylation of homocysteine to methionine, affecting S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) levels, a major methyl donor. We propose that reduced MTR activity diminishes SAM availability, decreasing DNA and histone methylation at promoters of CoQ10 biosynthetic genes. This epigenetic modification leads to reduced CoQ10 synthesis, contributing to primary coenzyme Q10 deficiency, type 2. To test this, we predict that cells with MTR knockdown or specific inhibitors will show lower SAM levels and hypomethylation at CoQ10 gene promoters, correlating with decreased CoQ10 production. Restoration of SAM should rescue CoQ10 synthesis, confirming the hypothesis. Conversely, unchanged promoter methylation and CoQ10 levels in response to MTR inhibition would refute the connection between MTR activity and CoQ10 biosynthesis regulation.

We hypothesize that the enzyme phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase 1 (PCK1) dysregulation directly contributes to the pathogenesis of Polyglucosan Body Myopathy 2 (PGBM2) by altering glycolytic flux and increasing glycogen branching. PCK1, a key enzyme in gluconeogenesis, modulates the levels of phosphoenolpyruvate. If its activity is reduced, it may lead to a compensatory increase in glycolytic activity. This shift could elevate the flux through glycogen synthase, increasing the production of poorly branched polyglucosan bodies, characteristic of PGBM2. We predict that overexpressing PCK1 in a cellular model of PGBM2 will decrease polyglucosan formation, while knockdown of PCK1 will exacerbate it. Confirmation would emerge from quantifying polyglucosan content using periodic acid-Schiff staining and observing a decrease in cells overexpressing PCK1, and an increase in PCK1-deficient cells. Refutation would occur if alterations in PCK1 levels do not affect polyglucosan body deposition.

We hypothesize that the enzyme UDP-galactose:ceramide galactosyltransferase 8 (UGT8) contributes to the pathogenesis of Rafiq syndrome through altered glycolipid metabolism leading to disrupted myelin sheath integrity. UGT8 is responsible for the galactosylation of ceramide, forming galactosylceramide, a crucial lipid component of myelin. In Rafiq syndrome, we propose that mutations in UGT8 result in decreased enzyme activity, leading to reduced galactosylceramide levels and, consequently, defective myelin formation. This mechanistic disruption may underlie the neurological manifestations of Rafiq syndrome. To test this hypothesis, we predict that fibroblasts or neural cells derived from Rafiq syndrome patients will show reduced UGT8 activity and lower galactosylceramide levels compared to controls. Conversely, normal UGT8 activity and galactosylceramide levels in these cells would refute our hypothesis. This could be experimentally tested using enzymatic activity assays and lipidomics analyses.

We hypothesize that GPX4 (Glutathione Peroxidase 4) plays a pivotal role in modulating oxidative stress and subsequent inflammatory pathways in juvenile arthritis by regulating ferroptosis in synovial fibroblasts. GPX4 reduces lipid hydroperoxides, preventing ferroptotic cell death. In juvenile arthritis, impaired GPX4 activity may lead to increased lipid peroxidation and ferroptosis, contributing to inflammation and joint damage. This mechanism suggests that diminished GPX4 function exacerbates synovial fibroblast death and inflammatory mediator release. To test this hypothesis, we predict that GPX4 knockdown in synovial fibroblasts will increase lipid peroxidation, biomarker expression of ferroptosis (e.g., ACSL4), and pro-inflammatory cytokines. Conversely, increased GPX4 activity via pharmacological inducers should reduce these indicators. Confirmation would support a protective role for GPX4 against oxidative stress in juvenile arthritis, while no change in ferroptosis or inflammation markers following GPX4 modulation would refute our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that the enzyme deoxyuridine triphosphatase (DUT) disrupts the nucleotide pool balance, leading to genomic instability that exacerbates Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, musculocontractural type 1 (EDS-MC1). DUT's role in hydrolyzing dUTP to dUMP is crucial for preventing uracil incorporation into DNA. In EDS-MC1, mutations in the CHST14 gene affect dermatan sulfate biosynthesis, resulting in connective tissue defects. We propose that decreased DUT activity leads to increased uracil incorporation, causing DNA repair stress and further weakening connective tissue integrity due to compromised genomic and cellular function. This can worsen the phenotypic severity of EDS-MC1. The hypothesis predicts that EDS-MC1 fibroblasts with downregulated DUT expression will exhibit higher levels of uracil in DNA, increased DNA repair biomarkers, and aggravated connective tissue abnormalities. Conversely, normalizing DUT expression or activity should reduce uracil misincorporation and partially restore connective tissue function, serving as a potential therapeutic approach.

We hypothesize that protein-O-mannose kinase (POMK) indirectly influences histidinemia by modulating cellular processes that impact histidine degradation pathways. Specifically, defects in POMK phosphorylation activity could impair the structure and function of a glycoprotein that interacts with histidine ammonia-lyase (HAL), the enzyme responsible for the conversion of histidine to urocanate. This impairment may lead to reduced HAL activity, resulting in the accumulation of histidine characteristic of histidinemia. We predict that in a cell model with knocked-down POMK expression, HAL activity will be significantly decreased compared to wild-type controls, contributing to higher histidine levels. Additionally, mass spectrometry could reveal altered glycosylation patterns of HAL-related glycoproteins. Conversely, if POMK knockdown does not affect HAL activity or histidine levels in these cells, this would refute our hypothesis. This connection aligns with POMK's known role in protein glycosylation and its potential impact on metabolic pathways.

We hypothesize that mutations in methionyl-tRNA synthetase 1 (MARS1) disrupt methionine-tRNA charging efficiency, impairing protein translation fidelity, and leading to aberrant keratinocyte function in Erythrokeratodermia variabilis et progressiva 4 (EKVP4). MARS1's role in catalyzing the attachment of methionine to its corresponding tRNA is crucial for initiating protein synthesis. In EKVP4, dysfunctional MARS1 may reduce methionine incorporation, affecting proteins critical for skin cellular homeostasis and keratin network formation. We predict that keratinocytes from EKVP4 patients will show reduced methionine-tRNA charging and decreased synthesis of structural skin proteins. Experimentally, mass spectrometry analysis in mutant keratinocytes will reveal a specific deficiency in methionine-initiated proteins, confirming our hypothesis. Refuting evidence would include unchanged methionine-tRNA charging or unaffected protein synthesis profiles in EKVP4 patient-derived cells compared to controls. This mechanistic insight could guide therapeutic focus on enhancing translation accuracy in EKVP4.

We hypothesize that LIPT1, an enzyme crucial for the lipoylation of 2-ketoacid dehydrogenase complexes, impacts the metabolic flux through amino acid catabolic pathways, indirectly influencing the histidine degradation pathway at the step involving histidase. In urocanase deficiency, impaired histidine catabolism leads to elevated levels of urocanic acid. We propose that partial dysfunction of LIPT1 reduces histidine breakdown precursors by impairing the branched-chain amino acid degradation, limiting substrates necessary for compensatory metabolic pathways that otherwise mitigate accumulated urocanic acid. To test this, we predict that LIPT1 suppression in a cell culture system will exacerbate urocanic acid accumulation when histidine is added to the medium, compared to controls. Conversely, augmented urocanic acid levels should not differ significantly from controls upon LIPT1 overexpression. This mechanistic link could be validated by quantifying intracellular urocanate levels using mass spectrometry following LIPT1 modulation, confirming LIPT1's role in exacerbating urocanase deficiency symptoms.

We hypothesize that purine nucleoside phosphorylase (PNP) contributes to the development of Fish-eye disease by disrupting phospholipid metabolism in the cornea. PNP, primarily known for purine metabolism, may influence cholesterol esterification pathways in the cornea through altered ATP levels and adenosine receptor signaling. This disruption could affect the activity of lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT), whose deficiency is linked to Fish-eye disease characterized by corneal opacification. Specifically, we propose that aberrant PNP activity leads to reduced ATP production, impairing LCAT-mediated cholesterol esterification and resulting in lipid accumulation in corneal tissues. A specific, falsifiable prediction is that PNP inhibition in corneal cell cultures will restore LCAT function and normalize lipid profiles, evidenced by decreased free cholesterol levels. Conversely, confirmation that PNP inhibition does not affect LCAT activity or lipid composition in these models would refute our hypothesis.

terminal_shown: Microcephaly, congenital cataract, and psoriasiform dermatitis
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that ALOX15 modulates the production of bioactive lipid mediators, influencing neural development and differentiation, and epidermal and lens homeostasis. ALOX15 catalyzes the formation of 15-Hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acid (15-HETE) from arachidonic acid, which can regulate signaling pathways critical for neurogenesis and epithelial cell function. Inadequate production of 15-HETE may impair neural progenitor cell proliferation, leading to microcephaly. Concurrently, insufficient 15-HETE levels may affect lens epithelial cell homeostasis, contributing to congenital cataracts, and disrupt keratinocyte differentiation and inflammation control, causing psoriasiform dermatitis. We predict that ALOX15-deficient models will show reduced 15-HETE levels, microcephaly-like phenotypes, lens opacity, and psoriasis-like skin lesions. Restoration of 15-HETE should alleviate these phenotypes. Conversely, normal phenotypes in ALOX15-deficient models would refute our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that MTHFD1 (methylenetetrahydrofolate dehydrogenase 1), which regulates one-carbon metabolism and mitochondrial folate cycle, plays a critical role in the development of sensorineural mitochondrial deafness by modulating mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) maintenance. Disruption in MTHFD1 activity could lead to impaired dNTP synthesis and imbalanced mitochondrial folate metabolism, resulting in increased susceptibility to oxidative damage and mtDNA mutations crucial for cochlear hair cell function. A specific testable prediction is that knocking down MTHFD1 expression in cochlear cell models will increase mtDNA damage, measured by quantitative PCR, and reduce ATP production, analyzed by luminescent assay. Confirmation would come from observing increased mtDNA lesions and decreased ATP levels post-MTHFD1 knockdown. Conversely, the hypothesis would be refuted if no significant increase in mtDNA damage or ATP reduction is observed, despite MTHFD1 downregulation, possibly indicating alternative compensatory pathways maintaining cochlear mitochondrial integrity.

We hypothesize that FDFT1 (squalene synthase), an enzyme critical in the cholesterol biosynthesis pathway, influences Gaucher disease by modulating glucocerebroside accumulation. Excess cholesterol is known to impact lysosomal storage disorders by altering lipid trafficking and storage. In Gaucher disease, caused by deficient activity of glucocerebrosidase, sphingolipid accumulation disrupts lysosomal function. We propose that increased FDFT1 activity elevates cholesterol levels, exacerbating the lysosomal storage of glucocerebrosides, worsening the cellular and clinical manifestations of Gaucher disease. To test this hypothesis, we would measure glucocerebroside levels in FDFT1-attenuated Gaucher disease cell models. Reduced glucocerebroside accumulation would support the hypothesis, while no change or an increase would refute it. This hypothesis grounds itself in the biochemical relationship between cholesterol metabolism and lysosomal storage diseases, offering a potential new target for therapeutic strategies in Gaucher disease through modulation of FDFT1 activity.

We hypothesize that EHHADH (Enoyl-CoA Hydratase and 3-Hydroxyacyl CoA Dehydrogenase) aberrantly interacts with the glutathione metabolism pathway, contributing to 5-oxoprolinase deficiency. Specifically, EHHADH may impact the beta-oxidation of fatty acids leading to altered levels of metabolic intermediates such as acyl-CoAs that inhibit normal 5-oxoprolinase function. This inhibition could disrupt the conversion of 5-oxoproline to glutamate, causing the accumulation of 5-oxoproline. Consequently, 5-oxoprolin accumulation leads to depleted glutathione levels and oxidative stress, characteristic of 5-oxoprolinase deficiency. To test this hypothesis, we would measure 5-oxoproline levels and glutathione status in cells with and without functional EHHADH expression. A confirmation would be an increase in 5-oxoproline and decrease in glutathione in cells lacking EHHADH, while EHHADH presence restores normal levels. If no significant changes are detected, it would refute the hypothesis, suggesting no involvement of EHHADH in modulating 5-oxoprolinase activity.

We hypothesize that CYP3A5 modulates neurodevelopmental processes contributing to Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy 71 (DEE71) by influencing the metabolism of neuroactive steroids. Specifically, CYP3A5 variants alter the metabolism of pregnenolone and progesterone, affecting the levels of neuroactive metabolites such as allopregnanolone, which are critical for neuronal excitability and synaptogenesis. We predict that individuals with DEE71 will exhibit aberrant CYP3A5-mediated steroid profiles compared to controls, leading to altered GABA_A receptor modulation and increased seizure susceptibility. This hypothesis can be tested by assessing neuroactive steroid levels in plasma and cerebrospinal fluid of DEE71 patients with different CYP3A5 genetic variants. A correlation between altered steroid profiles and seizure frequency would support the hypothesis, whereas no association would refute it. This connection is grounded in CYP3A5's known role in steroid metabolism and the importance of neurosteroids in neuronal functioning and epilepsy.

We hypothesize that the enzyme Arylsulfatase B (ARSB) contributes to congenital non-spherocytic hemolytic anemia 2 (CNSHA2) by impacting erythrocyte membrane stability through its role in the degradation of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs). ARSB deficiency may lead to the accumulation of dermatan sulfate, altering the sulfation pattern of GAGs present in erythrocyte membranes. This altered sulfation could increase membrane fragility, precipitating hemolysis. We predict that erythrocytes from CNSHA2 patients with suspected ARSB anomalies will exhibit significantly higher dermatan sulfate levels compared to controls, correlating with reduced membrane stability in osmotic fragility tests. Conversely, normal sulfate levels and typical membrane resilience in erythrocytes would refute this hypothesis. This hypothesis aligns with known ARSB function in GAG catabolism and suggests a novel mechanism whereby aberrant GAG processing affects erythrocyte integrity, leading to hemolytic anemia in CNSHA2.

We hypothesize that CYP2C9 modulates the severity of lecithin-cholesterol acyltransferase (LCAT) deficiency through its role in arachidonic acid metabolism, affecting inflammation and lipid homeostasis. Specifically, CYP2C9 converts arachidonic acid to hydroxyeicosatetraenoic acids (HETEs), influencing inflammatory pathways and altering the lipid environment critical for LCAT function. Inadequate conversion due to impaired CYP2C9 activity may exacerbate lipid imbalances inherent to LCAT deficiency, worsening the phenotype. To test this, we would inhibit CYP2C9 activity in a LCAT-deficient model and assess changes in lipid profile, inflammation, and disease severity. We predict that suppression of CYP2C9 will exacerbate lipid abnormalities and increase inflammation markers in LCAT-deficient subjects. Conversely, enhancement of CYP2C9 or compensatory pathways should attenuate these effects. Experimentally, confirmation would come from observing worse lipid and inflammatory profiles upon CYP2C9 inhibition in LCAT-deficient models, while refutation would arise if no such exacerbation is observed.

We hypothesize that GUSB (β-glucuronidase) is implicated in Leber congenital amaurosis 11 (LCA11) through disruption of glycosaminoglycan (GAG) turnover, leading to retinal cell dysfunction. GUSB is responsible for breaking down GAGs, which, if accumulated, may interfere with cellular signaling and homeostasis in the retinal cells. In LCA11, mutations in the GUSB gene may result in elevated GAG levels, disrupting the photoreceptor layer and causing retinal degeneration. We predict that in a retinal cell model with reduced GUSB expression, there will be accumulation of GAGs, leading to decreased photoreceptor response to light stimuli, detectable via electrophysiological assessments. Confirmation would require observing GAG accumulation and impaired retinal function in GUSB-deficient models specifically associated with LCA11 phenotypes. Refutation would involve normal GAG levels and photoreceptor function despite reduced GUSB activity, implying alternative pathways in LCA11 pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that IGF1R (insulin-like growth factor 1 receptor) dysfunction leads to neurodevelopmental abnormalities contributing to Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy 89 (DEE89) by impairing neuronal insulin signaling and synaptic plasticity. Specifically, aberrant autophosphorylation of IGF1R may disrupt downstream PI3K-AKT-mTOR pathways, crucial for neuronal survival and dendritic growth. This disruption may hinder neuronal network development, resulting in hyperexcitable circuits characteristic of DEE89. We predict that neurons derived from patient-derived iPSCs with mutated IGF1R would show reduced PI3K-AKT-mTOR signaling and compromised dendritic structure compared to healthy controls. Restoration of normal signaling from IGF1R activation via agonists would rescue these phenotypes. Conversely, further inhibition of IGF1R in these models should exacerbate the signaling deficiency and morphological defects, indicating a direct mechanistic link between IGF1R malfunction and DEE89 pathogenesis. This link could be validated using biochemical assays to measure pathway activity and detailed morphological analyses of neuronal cultures.

We hypothesize that LDHAL6A interacts with the N-terminal acetylation process by modulating the energy metabolism required for acetyltransferase function. LDHAL6A, primarily involved in lactate metabolism, may impact the cellular availability of Acetyl-CoA, a key substrate for N-terminal acetyltransferases. In N-terminal acetyltransferase deficiency, a reduction in Acetyl-CoA due to altered LDHAL6A activity could exacerbate acetylation disruptions, impacting protein stability and function. We predict that in cells deficient in N-terminal acetyltransferase, overexpressing LDHAL6A will rescue some acetylation-dependent pathways by normalizing Acetyl-CoA levels, as measured by increased levels of properly acetylated proteins. Conversely, knocking down LDHAL6A in these deficient cells will worsen the acetylation deficiency, showing decreased Acetyl-CoA and acetylated proteins. This hypothesis is supported by LDHAL6A's role in metabolic pathways influencing co-factor availability, integral to acetylation processes.

We hypothesize that AMPD1 (Adenosine monophosphate deaminase 1) contributes to acyl-CoA dehydrogenase very long-chain deficiency (VLCADD) by modulating adenosine monophosphate (AMP) levels, impacting mitochondrial energy balance and fatty acid oxidation. We propose that the reduced activity of AMPD1 leads to an accumulation of AMP, which activates AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK). Elevated AMPK suppresses mitochondrial fatty acid import and oxidation by phosphorylating acetyl-CoA carboxylase, increasing malonyl-CoA levels, and inhibiting carnitine palmitoyltransferase 1. This exacerbates VLCADD pathology by further impairing very long-chain fatty acid oxidation, a primary defect in this disease. We predict that specific AMPD1 inhibition in VLCADD models will worsen fatty acid metabolism disturbances, observable via reduced β-oxidation rates and increased long-chain acyl-carnitine accumulation. Conversely, stabilizing AMPD1 activity should alleviate these metabolic disruptions. Experimental validation involves measuring fatty acid oxidation intermediates and AMPK activity in VLCADD models with modified AMPD1 function.

We hypothesize that MRI1 (Methylthioribose-1-phosphate isomerase), a key enzyme in the methionine salvage pathway, is mechanistically connected to RENI syndrome through disruptions in methionine homeostasis. MRI1 catalyzes the isomerization of methylthioribose-1-phosphate to methylthioribulose-1-phosphate, a critical step in recycling methionine, an amino acid vital for methylation reactions and cellular redox balance. In RENI syndrome, characterized by neurodevelopmental and metabolic abnormalities, we propose that MRI1 dysfunction leads to impaired methionine recycling, resulting in altered S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) levels, affecting gene expression and epigenetic regulation. A falsifiable prediction is that patients with RENI syndrome will exhibit significantly reduced MRI1 activity and altered SAM levels compared to controls, which could be measured in blood samples. Confirmation of this hypothesis would show reduced SAM and altered global DNA methylation patterns in patient's biopsies, while refutation would show unchanged MRI1 activity and SAM levels in RENI syndrome patients.

We hypothesize that the enzyme A4GALT, responsible for synthesizing the glycosphingolipid Gb3, contributes to male pseudohermaphroditism with gynecomastia through disrupted hormone regulation. Specifically, overexpression or enhanced activity of A4GALT may lead to excessive Gb3 accumulation, which impairs androgen receptor (AR) signaling due to altered lipid raft compositions in cell membranes. This disruption reduces testosterone response, crucial for male sexual differentiation, leading to pseudohermaphroditism. Furthermore, Gb3 accumulation may activate alternative signaling pathways involving estrogen receptors, promoting gynecomastia. This hypothesis could be tested by comparing Gb3 levels and AR signaling activity in cell lines or animal models with overexpressed A4GALT against normal controls. A confirmed prediction would show increased Gb3 levels and disrupted AR signaling in these models, while normal levels and unaffected AR signaling in controls would refute it. This pathway illustrates a specific molecular mechanism linking A4GALT activity to the target disease phenotype.

We hypothesize that decreased DHCR24 activity exacerbates the neurological manifestations of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome through dysregulated cholesterol biosynthesis, impairing membrane integrity and neurotransmitter receptor function. DHCR24, an enzyme involved in converting desmosterol to cholesterol, intersects with purine metabolism disrupted in Lesch-Nyhan syndrome due to HPRT deficiency. We propose this results in altered neuronal membrane cholesterol, affecting synaptic transmission and contributing to neurobehavioral symptoms. Confirmatory evidence would include observing diminished membrane cholesterol content alongside impaired synaptic function in neuronal cells deficient in both HPRT and DHCR24 activity, compared to HPRT-deficient cells alone. Conversely, normal synaptic function and cholesterol levels in these cells would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism bridges abnormal lipid metabolism and neurological phenotypes typical of Lesch-Nyhan syndrome, supported by the critical role of balanced cholesterol levels in neuronal health.

We hypothesize that PCYT2, an enzyme integral to phosphatidylethanolamine biosynthesis, indirectly modulates insulin secretion in pancreatic β-cells by influencing endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane composition. In Hyperinsulinemic hypoglycemia, familial, 4, characterized by excessive insulin release, altered phosphatidylethanolamine levels due to dysfunctional PCYT2 could disrupt ER calcium dynamics and insulin granule handling. Specifically, reduced PCYT2 expression may lead to altered membrane fluidity, affecting calcium-dependent exocytotic proteins and amplifying insulin secretion in response to normal glucose levels. To test this, we predict that PCYT2 knockdown in pancreatic β-cells will result in increased insulin secretion under basal glucose conditions, attributable to aberrant ER-membrane composition and calcium homeostasis alterations. Confirmation would involve observing both increased insulin release and altered phosphatidylethanolamine in PCYT2-deficient cells. Refutation would be the absence of increased insulin secretion or phosphatidylethanolamine changes upon PCYT2 knockdown, indicating another pathway governs exaggerated β-cell response in the disease.

We hypothesize that PGAM4 (phosphoglycerate mutase family member 4), typically known for its role in glycolysis, aberrantly influences the biosynthesis of sialic acids in Sialuria by interacting with and stabilizing GNE (UDP-N-acetylglucosamine-2-epimerase/N-acetylmannosamine kinase), the key regulatory enzyme in sialic acid biosynthesis. In Sialuria, mutations in the GNE gene lead to overproduction of sialic acid. We propose that increased expression or stabilization of PGAM4 exacerbates sialic acid production by enhancing GNE activity. To test this, we predict that PGAM4 overexpression in a cellular model of Sialuria will increase sialic acid levels beyond levels observed with the GNE mutation alone. Conversely, silencing PGAM4 should normalize or reduce sialic acid accumulation compared to controls. This outcome would support the hypothesis, while a lack of change in sialic acid levels with PGAM4 manipulation would refute it, demonstrating no mechanistic link with PGAM4 in Sialuria.

terminal_shown: Progressive external ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA deletions, autosomal recessive 4
hypothesis_text:
We hypothesize that PMAIP1 (also known as NOXA), a pro-apoptotic member of the BCL-2 protein family, contributes to the pathogenesis of Progressive External Ophthalmoplegia with mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) deletions, autosomal recessive 4, by influencing mitochondrial quality control and apoptosis pathways. Specifically, we propose that PMAIP1 overexpression leads to excessive mitochondrial apoptosis, thereby enhancing the susceptibility to mtDNA deletions in muscle cells. This results in impaired oxidative phosphorylation, contributing to the characteristic muscular weakness and dysfunction observed in the disease. 

To test this hypothesis, we would overexpress PMAIP1 in cultured myoblasts derived from patient fibroblasts and assess for increased rates of mitochondrial apoptosis and mtDNA deletions compared to controls. Confirmation would entail finding elevated apoptotic markers and mtDNA deletions. Refutation would involve no significant change in these markers despite PMAIP1 overexpression. This mechanism links PMAIP1's role in apoptosis to the specific disease phenotype of mitochondrial dysfunction.

We hypothesize that the enzyme B3GAT3 (beta-1,3-glucuronyltransferase 3) contributes to Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome 2 by disrupting the synthesis of proteoglycans in the extracellular matrix. B3GAT3 is crucial for the assembly of glycosaminoglycans (GAGs), which are pivotal for cell signaling and structural integrity in neural tissues. Impaired B3GAT3 activity may lead to defective GAG biosynthesis, resulting in aberrant neuronal development and synaptic function, contributing to the neurological symptoms observed in the syndrome. This hypothesis predicts that individuals with the disease would show reduced B3GAT3 expression or activity, alongside altered GAG composition in neural tissues compared to healthy controls. Confirmation would come from experiments demonstrating a correlation between reduced B3GAT3 function and altered GAG synthesis in patient-derived neuronal cells or brain tissue. Refutation would involve normal GAG levels and neuronal function despite reduced B3GAT3 activity in affected individuals.

We hypothesize that MCAT (malonyl-CoA-acyl carrier protein transacylase) contributes to Immunodeficiency with hyper-IgM 2 by disrupting fatty acid synthesis required for proper B cell function. MCAT catalyzes the transfer of malonyl-CoA to acyl carrier protein, a crucial step in mitochondrial fatty acid biosynthesis. Impairment in MCAT activity could lead to altered membrane lipid composition in B cells, affecting their proliferation and antibody class switching, specifically impeding IgM to IgG conversion. We predict that B cells from patients with hyper-IgM 2 will exhibit abnormal lipid profiles and reduced IgG production due to faulty MCAT activity. Confirmation would come from observing reduced MCAT activity in patient-derived B cells and restoration of IgG production upon MCAT supplementation. Refutation would occur if MCAT activity is normal and IgG switching is unresponsive to MCAT modulation in vitro. This suggests MCAT's role in B cell membrane biosynthesis as a novel immunodeficiency mechanism.

We hypothesize that ALDH9A1, an aldehyde dehydrogenase involved in γ-aminobutyric acid (GABA) metabolism, contributes to congenital myasthenic syndrome 12 (CMS12) by impairing neurotransmitter balance at the neuromuscular junction. ALDH9A1 oxidizes γ-aminobutyraldehyde to GABA, a key inhibitory neurotransmitter modulating synaptic transmission. A deficiency in ALDH9A1 may lead to GABA depletion, disrupting the excitation-inhibition balance critical for neuromuscular function. This imbalance may diminish acetylcholine release or impair postsynaptic receptor sensitivity, contributing to the muscle weakness characteristic of CMS12. We predict that ALDH9A1-deficient pathways in muscle biopsies from CMS12 patients will exhibit reduced GABA levels and altered neuromuscular junction function. Confirmation would involve finding decreased GABA and heightened muscle fatigue in ALDH9A1-deficient CMS12 models, while normal GABA and muscle function in genetically unmodified models would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that NDUFS3, a core subunit of mitochondrial Complex I, contributes to the pathogenesis of Retinitis pigmentosa 17 (RP17) through impaired electron transport and subsequent reactive oxygen species (ROS) overproduction, leading to photoreceptor cell apoptosis. Specifically, NDUFS3 mutations may reduce Complex I activity, diminishing ATP production and increasing ROS levels in retinal cells. This oxidative stress is predicted to activate apoptotic signaling pathways, resulting in progressive photoreceptor degeneration typical of RP17. We predict that retinal cells from RP17 patients will exhibit decreased NDUFS3 levels, lowered Complex I activity, and elevated ROS compared to controls. Conversely, restoring NDUFS3 function via gene therapy should normalize ROS levels and retard photoreceptor loss. Confirmation involves demonstrating reduced apoptosis in treated retinal cultures, while failure to observe these changes would refute the hypothesis. This mechanism aligns with biochemistry knowledge linking mitochondrial dysfunction to retinopathy.

We hypothesize that DHCR24 (24-dehydrocholesterol reductase) dysfunction contributes to Multiple congenital anomalies-hypotonia-seizures syndrome 2 (MCAHS2) by disrupting cholesterol biosynthesis. DHCR24 catalyzes the reduction of desmosterol to cholesterol, a critical step in neuronal membrane formation and myelination. Impaired DHCR24 activity leads to desmosterol accumulation and insufficient cholesterol levels, affecting neuron development and function. This disrupts neural connectivity and synaptic transmission, potentially causing MCAHS2's neurological symptoms. We predict that patients with MCAHS2 will exhibit elevated desmosterol and reduced cholesterol in neural tissue. Experiments using DHCR24 knockout models should reproduce MCAHS2 phenotypes, while supplementation with cholesterol precursors could rescue these. Conversely, normal DHCR24 function or exclusive cholesterol deficiency models should fail to replicate the full spectrum of MCAHS2 features, refuting the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that the enzyme NDUFB3, a component of complex I in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, is mechanistically linked to RENI syndrome through impaired oxidative phosphorylation. In RENI syndrome, neurological and immunological symptoms align with disrupted energy metabolism in neurons and immune cells. NDUFB3 dysfunction could lead to reduced NADH oxidation, decreased ATP production, and increased reactive oxygen species (ROS), causing neuronal and immune cell dysfunction. We predict that cells from RENI syndrome patients will show reduced complex I activity, decreased ATP levels, and increased ROS compared to controls. If modifying NDUFB3 expression in vitro restores complex I function and alleviates these cellular defects, our hypothesis is confirmed; if no change occurs, it is refuted. This hypothesis highlights the potential of targeting NDUFB3-related pathways for therapeutic intervention in RENI syndrome.

terminal_shown: Skeletal dysplasia, mild, with joint laxity and advanced bone age
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in the enzyme ACADSB (acyl-CoA dehydrogenase, short/branched chain), which is involved in the mitochondrial β-oxidation of branched-chain fatty acids, lead to the accumulation of toxic intermediates that disrupt chondrocyte metabolism, contributing to skeletal dysplasia, mild, with joint laxity and advanced bone age. Specifically, we propose that impaired ACADSB activity causes an accumulation of isobutyryl-CoA and other by-products, leading to oxidative stress and metabolic dysregulation in chondrocytes, thereby affecting collagen maturation and extracellular matrix organization crucial for normal cartilage and bone development. To confirm this hypothesis, experimental validation could involve ACADSB knockdown in chondrocyte cultures and observing increased isobutyryl-CoA levels with concurrent oxidative stress markers and disrupted collagen maturation. This prediction would be refuted if ACADSB knockdown does not alter these metabolic and cellular parameters, thereby not yielding the pathological features characteristic of skeletal dysplasia with joint laxity and advanced bone age.

We hypothesize that the enzyme Prostaglandin-endoperoxide synthase 1 (PTGS1), also known as Cyclooxygenase-1 (COX-1), contributes to the pathogenesis of acute transient encephalopathy through its role in the synthesis of prostaglandins, which mediate neuroinflammatory responses. Specifically, excessive activity of PTGS1 may lead to increased production of prostaglandin E2 (PGE2), promoting inflammation and vasodilation in the central nervous system. This could disrupt the blood-brain barrier and result in transient neuronal dysfunction, characteristic of acute transient encephalopathy. To test this hypothesis, we would predict that inhibition of PTGS1 activity in an animal model of acute transient encephalopathy would result in a decrease in PGE2 levels and an attenuation of neurological symptoms. Conversely, if PTGS1 activity is irrelevant, then PTGS1 inhibitors would have no significant effect on PGE2 levels or neurological outcomes, thereby refuting our hypothesis. This connection is grounded in PTGS1’s known role in prostaglandin synthesis and its implications in neuroinflammation.

We hypothesize that the enzyme TRY-GTA7-1 contributes to the pathogenesis of Farber lipogranulomatosis by aberrantly modulating ceramide metabolism. TRY-GTA7-1 may function as an atypical ceramidase, converting ceramides into sphingosine at an abnormal rate or location, leading to an accumulation of ceramide in lysosomes. This accumulation triggers the pathological inflammation and granuloma formation characteristic of Farber lipogranulomatosis. The hypothesis predicts that silencing or inhibiting TRY-GTA7-1 activity in a cellular model of Farber disease will result in decreased ceramide levels and reduced inflammatory cytokine release. Conversely, overexpression of TRY-GTA7-1 should exacerbate ceramide accumulation and inflammation. Verification experiments could involve using mass spectrometry to quantify ceramide levels and ELISA for cytokine measurements post-manipulation of TRY-GTA7-1 expression. A failure to observe changes in ceramide metabolism or inflammatory responses upon modulation of TRY-GTA7-1 would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that ACACA (acetyl-CoA carboxylase alpha) influences Fabry disease pathogenesis through lipogenesis dysregulation, exacerbating lipid substrate accumulation in lysosomes. In Fabry disease, the deficiency of α-galactosidase A leads to globotriaosylceramide (Gb3) accumulation. Aberrant ACACA activity could alter acetyl-CoA levels and increase malonyl-CoA, promoting excessive fatty acid synthesis and disrupting lipid homeostasis. This imbalance may further inhibit lipophagy, a process crucial for degrading accumulated Gb3 in lysosomes, thereby accelerating Gb3 deposition. Experimentally, we predict that ACACA inhibition will reduce Gb3 accumulation in Fabry disease cellular models. Consistent with this, treatment with an ACC inhibitor should result in decreased Gb3 levels compared to untreated controls. Conversely, increased Gb3 accumulation despite ACC inhibition would refute our hypothesis. This proposal aligns with known roles of ACACA in lipid metabolism and provides a mechanistic link potentially exploitable for Fabry disease therapeutic intervention.

We hypothesize that PTK2, also known as focal adhesion kinase (FAK), contributes to the pathogenesis of Developmental and Epileptic Encephalopathy 84 (DEE84) by dysregulating synaptic stability and neuronal signaling. Specifically, we propose that aberrant activation of PTK2 impairs integrin-mediated signaling pathways, leading to altered dendritic spine morphology and synaptic transmission in neurons, which are crucial during neurodevelopment. This dysregulation would result in neuronal hyperexcitability contributing to the epileptic encephalopathy characteristic of DEE84. We predict that knockdown or pharmacological inhibition of PTK2 in a DEE84 model will restore normal synaptic architecture and reduce hyperexcitability, evidenced by restored dendritic spine density and decreased seizure frequency. Conversely, overexpression of PTK2 will exacerbate synaptic abnormalities and seizure activity. Confirming this hypothesis requires observing these synaptic and electrophysiological corrections or exacerbations in response to modulating PTK2 activity in relevant neuronal models.

We hypothesize that CEPT1, a key enzyme in phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, contributes to Retinitis pigmentosa 53 by disrupting photoreceptor cell membrane integrity through altered phospholipid composition. CEPT1 catalyzes the transfer of phosphocholine to diacylglycerol, forming phosphatidylcholine, a major component of cell membranes. Inadequate CEPT1 activity may lead to an imbalanced lipid ratio, affecting membrane fluidity and disrupting photoreceptor disc renewal processes critical for retinal function. This alteration could trigger apoptosis of photoreceptor cells, a hallmark of Retinitis pigmentosa 53. To test this hypothesis, we predict that retinal tissues from patients with Retinitis pigmentosa 53 will show reduced CEPT1 activity and altered phosphatidylcholine levels. Confirmation would include demonstrating photoreceptor degeneration parallel to phospholipid imbalance in a CEPT1 knockdown model. Refutation would occur if CEPT1 activity and phosphatidylcholine levels are unchanged in these tissues, suggesting an alternative pathway.

terminal_shown: Hypercarotenemia and vitamin A deficiency, autosomal dominant
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that mutations in the enzyme Methylthioribose-1-phosphate Isomerase 1 (MRI1) alter its role in the methionine salvage pathway, disrupting the conversion of methylthioribose phosphate to methionine, which is crucial for proper retinoid metabolism. This disruption leads to impaired beta-carotene conversion to vitamin A, resulting in hypercarotenemia and autosomal dominant vitamin A deficiency. Specifically, we predict that mutant MRI1 decreases methionine availability, impairing the synthesis of methionine-dependent enzymes needed for efficient vitamin A conversion. A confirmatory experiment would demonstrate decreased methionine levels and reduced activity of retinal-based enzymes in cells expressing mutant MRI1 compared to wild-type. Additionally, supplementation with exogenous methionine should rescue these deficiencies. Conversely, if methionine levels and enzyme activities remain unchanged or unaffected by methionine supplementation in mutant conditions, the hypothesis would be refuted.

terminal_shown: Combined deficiency of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors 1
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that BAK1 (BCL2 Antagonist/Killer 1) indirectly contributes to the pathogenesis of Combined Deficiency of Vitamin K-dependent Clotting Factors 1 (VKCFD1) by modulating apoptosis in hepatocytes, which alters vitamin K metabolism. BAK1, known to regulate apoptosis, may impact liver cell survival; liver dysfunction could impair gamma-carboxylation of clotting factors, a vitamin K-dependent process. We propose that increased BAK1 activity leads to heightened hepatocyte apoptosis, reducing the synthesis of vitamin K-dependent clotting factors. Experimental prediction: Overexpression of BAK1 in hepatocyte cultures will reduce levels of gamma-carboxylase and vitamin K-dependent clotting factors (e.g., prothrombin). Detection of decreased clotting factor levels in BAK1-overexpressing liver tissue models (compared to controls) would confirm this hypothesis. Conversely, unaltered gamma-carboxylase activity and clotting factor levels, despite BAK1 modulation, would refute the proposed mechanism. This connects BAK1's apoptotic role to VKCFD1 pathophysiology.

terminal_shown: Neurodevelopmental disorder, mitochondrial, with abnormal movements and lactic acidosis, with or without seizures
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that the enzyme UDP-galactose-4'-epimerase (GALE) plays a critical role in the development of neurodevelopmental disorder, mitochondrial, with abnormal movements and lactic acidosis, with or without seizures, through its influence on glycosylation patterns affecting mitochondrial function. Specifically, impaired GALE activity may lead to aberrant glycosylation of mitochondrial proteins, disrupting their function and leading to inefficient oxidative phosphorylation. This would result in increased production of lactic acid and metabolic stress, contributing to the observed neurodevelopmental and movement abnormalities. This hypothesis predicts that in cell models with reduced GALE activity, we will observe altered glycosylation patterns on mitochondrial proteins, decreased mitochondrial respiratory efficiency, and increased lactate production compared to controls. Confirmation of such changes would support the hypothesis, while normal glycosylation and mitochondrial function in these models would refute it, suggesting an alternate mechanism for the disease's pathology.

We hypothesize that GGPS1 (geranylgeranyl diphosphate synthase 1) plays a critical role in Yunis-Varon syndrome (YVS) via impaired prenylation of small GTPases, crucial for bone development and cellular trafficking. GGPS1 is essential for synthesizing geranylgeranyl diphosphate, which modifies proteins through prenylation. We propose that mutations or dysfunction in GGPS1 lead to defective prenylation of small GTPases like Rab and Rho, disrupting vesicular trafficking and cytoskeletal organization. This results in the impaired osteoblastic activity and neural anomalies seen in YVS. A specific prediction is that fibroblasts from YVS patients will exhibit reduced prenylation of small GTPases, observable through mass spectrometry and functional assays, compared to controls. Confirming this reduced prenylation would support our hypothesis, while normal prenylation patterns would refute it, suggesting an alternate pathway is responsible for linking GGPS1 with YVS.

We hypothesize that the enzyme hydroxymethylbilane synthase (HMBS), crucial for heme biosynthesis, indirectly contributes to muscular dystrophy, limb-girdle, autosomal recessive 21 (LGMDR21) by affecting muscle mitochondrial function. HMBS deficiency may lead to reduced heme levels, impairing cytochrome c oxidase activity and disrupting mitochondrial electron transport, which could diminish ATP production necessary for muscle function. This energetic deficit might exacerbate muscle fiber damage and weakness characteristic of LGMDR21. To test this, we propose measuring mitochondrial respiration and cytochrome c oxidase activity in muscle biopsies from LGMDR21 patients with known HMBS mutations. Reduced mitochondrial function compared to controls would support our hypothesis. Conversely, normal mitochondrial function in these patients would refute the connection. This hypothesis aligns with known biochemistry of heme's role in mitochondrial integrity and offers a novel link to LGMDR21 pathophysiology.

We hypothesize that Stearoyl-CoA desaturase (SCD), by modulating lipid metabolism, contributes to the pathogenesis of Cocoon syndrome, a rare fibrotic condition. SCD catalyzes the desaturation of saturated fatty acids into monounsaturated fatty acids, crucial for membrane fluidity and cell signaling. Dysfunctional SCD activity may lead to an abnormal fatty acid profile, promoting excessive deposition and maturation of extracellular matrix proteins, thus inducing tissue fibrosis observed in Cocoon syndrome. A specific, falsifiable prediction is that patients with Cocoon syndrome will exhibit altered SCD expression or activity levels, alongside an aberrant monounsaturated to saturated fatty acid ratio in fibroblast cultures from affected tissues. Confirmatory experimental results would show increased fibrosis and disrupted lipid profiles in SCD-overexpressing cell models. Conversely, SCD knockdown should normalize lipid profiles and reduce fibrosis markers. Refuting evidence would include unchanged fibrosis levels and lipid metabolic profiles irrespective of SCD activity modulation.

We hypothesize that the enzyme alkaline phosphatase, intestinal (ALPI), modulates sulfur metabolism and thus impacts the keratin structure in individuals with Trichothiodystrophy 8, non-photosensitive (TTD8). ALPI may influence cysteine homeostasis by dephosphorylating key intermediates in sulfur amino acid pathways, affecting keratin cross-linking in hair. Disrupted cysteine cycling could lead to the reduced sulfur content in hair shafts, a hallmark of TTD8. Experimentally, knocking down ALPI expression in organoid models of human hair follicles should reduce cysteine levels and disrupt keratin structure, akin to TTD8 phenotypes. Conversely, overexpressing ALPI should restore cysteine levels and normalize keratin cross-linking. This hypothesis can be tested by assessing hair sulfur content and structural integrity following ALPI manipulation. The finding of altered keratin structure directly correlated with ALPI activity alterations would support the hypothesis, whereas unchanged structural attributes would refute it, indicating that ALPI does not directly influence TTD8 pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that the enzyme glutamate-cysteine ligase catalytic subunit (GCLC) plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia by affecting glutathione synthesis and redox homeostasis in osteoblasts. GCLC is essential for synthesizing glutathione, a major cellular antioxidant. Inadequate GCLC activity may lead to insufficient glutathione levels, resulting in oxidative stress that impairs osteoblast differentiation and function. This could contribute to the skeletal dysplasia characteristic of Ghosal hematodiaphyseal dysplasia. To confirm this hypothesis, we predict that osteoblasts from affected individuals will demonstrate significantly decreased GCLC activity and glutathione levels compared to controls, alongside markers of oxidative stress and impaired differentiation. Conversely, restoring GCLC function in these cells, either genetically or pharmacologically, should normalize glutathione levels, reduce oxidative stress, and improve osteoblast function. A failure to observe these differences and effects would refute our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that BAK1, a pro-apoptotic Bcl-2 family member, contributes to the pathogenesis of Anterior Segment Dysgenesis 6 (ASD6) through the dysregulation of apoptosis in cranial neural crest cells (CNCCs) during eye development. Specifically, abnormal activation of BAK1 could lead to increased apoptosis of CNCCs that are critical for anterior segment structures such as the cornea and iris. This would result in developmental defects characteristic of ASD6. To test this hypothesis, a conditional knockout of BAK1 in CNCCs in a murine model would lead to reduced apoptosis, resulting in normal anterior segment development, thereby refuting the hypothesis if anomalies persist. Conversely, increased apoptosis and ASD6-like features in wild-type mice, exacerbated by BAK1 overexpression in CNCCs, would confirm the hypothesis. This hypothesis links BAK1-mediated apoptotic pathways to ASD6, providing a potential target for therapeutic intervention.

We hypothesize that the enzyme N-acetylglucosamine kinase (NAGK) contributes to Gillessen-Kaesbach-Nishimura syndrome (GKN syndrome) through disruption of glycosaminoglycan (GAG) biosynthesis. NAGK phosphorylates N-acetylglucosamine, a precursor for GAG synthesis. In GKN syndrome, a mutation or reduced activity of NAGK could lead to insufficient GAG production, impairing extracellular matrix formation critical for normal development and function. This defect may result in the skeletal and craniofacial anomalies characteristic of GKN syndrome. To test this hypothesis, we propose measuring GAG levels and examining extracellular matrix integrity in fibroblasts from GKN syndrome patients compared to controls. Reduced GAG levels and altered matrix structure in patient cells would confirm our hypothesis, while normal GAG levels and extracellular matrix integrity would refute it. Verification could also involve rescuing GAG synthesis via NAGK overexpression or supplementation of downstream metabolic intermediates in affected cells.

We hypothesize that the enzyme D-amino acid oxidase (DAO) influences Hypotrichosis 14 through its modulation of hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) levels, affecting hair follicle homeostasis. DAO catalyzes the oxidative deamination of D-amino acids, producing H2O2 as a byproduct. Elevated H2O2 can disrupt antioxidant defense and damage proteins in hair follicle cells. The hypothesis predicts that upregulation of DAO causes increased H2O2 in hair follicles, impairing keratinocyte function and leading to hypoplasia characteristic of Hypotrichosis 14. Conversely, DAO inhibition should normalize H2O2 levels and restore follicle function. To confirm this, elevated H2O2 and DAO activity should be observable in scalp biopsies from Hypotrichosis 14 patients compared to controls. In contrast, DAO inhibition in patient-derived follicle organoids should reduce H2O2 levels and improve keratinocyte structure, which, if not observed, would refute this hypothesis.

We hypothesize that cytochrome c oxidase subunit 6A1 (COX6A1) modulates oxidative phosphorylation efficiency, influencing the buildup of toxic metabolites in Tyrosinemia 1. Specifically, COX6A1 alters mitochondrial electron transport chain activity, affecting hepatic energy balance and the detoxification processes that are impaired due to faulty fumarylacetoacetate hydrolase (FAH) in Tyrosinemia 1. Reduced COX6A1 expression leads to less efficient ATP production, exacerbating the accumulation of succinylacetone, a metabolic intermediate in tyrosine catabolism, by inhibiting compensatory energy pathways. Our hypothesis predicts that mice with specific liver knockdown of COX6A1 will display increased sucinylacetone levels and liver dysfunction similar to Tyrosinemia 1 patients. Conversely, upregulation of COX6A1 in FAH-deficient models should exhibit partial restoration of mitochondrial function and a decrease in toxic metabolite accumulation, thus refuting the hypothesis if no such changes are observed.

We hypothesize that the GNAS enzyme, which modulates cyclic AMP (cAMP) signaling via its role as a G protein α-subunit, influences eosinophil peroxidase (EPO) enzyme expression and activity through the cAMP/Protein Kinase A (PKA) pathway. Specifically, decreased GNAS activity may result in lower cAMP levels, reducing PKA activation. This impairs the transcription of EPO gene, leading to Eosinophil peroxidase deficiency. To test this, we could compare EPO expression and activity in eosinophils with inhibited GNAS versus controls. A specific prediction is that GNAS inhibition will lead to significantly reduced EPO mRNA levels and enzyme activity. Confirmation of our hypothesis would involve observing this reduction, whereas no change in EPO expression after GNAS inhibition would refute it. Given the known regulatory role of cAMP/PKA pathway in gene expression, this hypothesis offers a plausible mechanistic link between GNAS and EPO deficiency.

We hypothesize that deficiency or aberrant activity of the glycogen branching enzyme GBE1 disrupts the structural integrity of glycogen in chondrocytes and ocular tissues, leading to the accumulation of improperly branched glycogen. This results in cellular stress and apoptosis, contributing to the phenotypic manifestations of Spondyloocular syndrome, such as skeletal deformities and ocular abnormalities. To test this, we propose evaluating glycogen structure and cellular health in patient-derived chondrocyte and retinal cell models with GBE1 mutations. If our hypothesis is correct, these cells will show altered glycogen structure and increased markers of endoplasmic reticulum stress and apoptosis compared to wild-type cells. Conversely, if GBE1 function does not influence these cellular processes, no significant difference in glycogen structure or stress markers will be observed between mutant and wild-type cells. This would refute the hypothesis by suggesting an alternative pathway or mechanism is involved in disease etiology.

We hypothesize that the enzyme CNPY3-GNMT, known for its role in glycine N-methylation and regulation of SAM/SAH ratio, affects androgen synthesis pathways during embryonic development, contributing to Pseudovaginal perineoscrotal hypospadias. Specifically, CNPY3-GNMT may modulate the availability of S-adenosylmethionine (SAM) required for the methylation of genes essential for proper androgen receptor activity and testosterone biosynthesis. Disruption in CNPY3-GNMT expression or function could lead to reduced SAM levels, impairing methylation-dependent gene activation, subsequently diminishing androgen production and signaling. To confirm this hypothesis, we predict that knockout or knockdown of CNPY3-GNMT in fetal testicular cells will result in decreased testosterone synthesis and abnormal genital development in a mammalian model. Conversely, overexpression of CNPY3-GNMT should correct or prevent hypospadias phenotypes due to restored androgen signaling. This hypothesis is grounded in the established role of SAM in methylation processes essential for hormone-dependent developmental pathways.

We hypothesize that the enzyme EHMT2 (euchromatic histone lysine methyltransferase 2) contributes to Porokeratosis 1, multiple types, by dysregulating keratinocyte differentiation through aberrant histone methylation. EHMT2 methylates histone H3 on lysine 9 (H3K9me2), typically repressing gene expression. In keratinocytes, excessive EHMT2 activity may lead to hypermethylation of promoter regions for genes crucial in epidermal differentiation, such as involucrin or loricrin. This epigenetic silencing could impair the formation of the stratum corneum, manifesting as dysfunctional keratinization observed in porokeratosis.

We predict that knockdown of EHMT2 in keratinocyte cultures will restore normal expression of differentiation genes and ameliorate hyperkeratotic features in a porokeratosis model. Conversely, overexpression of EHMT2 should exacerbate these features. Confirmation would come from chromatin immunoprecipitation followed by sequencing (ChIP-seq) showing reduced H3K9me2 at affected gene sites post-knockdown, while refutation would see no impact on methylation or gene expression from altered EHMT2 expression.

We hypothesize that PPA2, a mitochondrial pyrophosphatase, indirectly influences the accumulation of homogentisic acid (HGA) in alkaptonuria through dysregulated ATP levels affecting HGA oxidase activity. Under normal conditions, PPA2 hydrolyzes inorganic pyrophosphate to ensure optimal mitochondrial ATP production. In alkaptonuria, a reduced PPA2 activity might lead to diminished ATP availability, impairing ATP-dependent enzymatic processes, including those involving HGA oxidase, indirectly contributing to HGA buildup characteristic of alkaptonuria. 

To confirm, decreased PPA2 activity should correlate with reduced mitochondrial ATP levels and correspondingly decreased HGA oxidase activity in models of alkaptonuria. Additionally, restoration of ATP levels should normalize HGA oxidase activity despite low PPA2. Conversely, maintenance of mitochondrial ATP levels in the absence of functional PPA2 but with unaffected HGA oxidase activity would refute the hypothesis, indicating alternative pathways predominate in influencing HGA accumulation.

terminal_shown: Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with dystonia
hypothesis_text: We hypothesize that the enzyme DHRSX (Dehydrogenase/Reductase X-linked) influences the pathogenesis of Leber hereditary optic neuropathy with dystonia by modulating mitochondrial redox states and reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. DHRSX is posited to alter the activity of the mitochondrial electron transport chain, specifically at Complex I, wherein mutations are frequently associated with the disease. The hypothesis predicts that decreased DHRSX activity leads to impaired NADH turnover, increased ROS production, and subsequent oxidative damage to retinal ganglion cells and dystonia-related neural circuits. Experimentally, this hypothesis predicts that DHRSX knockdown in cellular models will result in elevated ROS levels and Complex I dysfunction, corroborated by increased oxidative stress markers. Conversely, overexpression should normalize ROS levels and improve Complex I efficiency. Falsification would occur if DHRSX manipulation does not significantly alter redox balance or ROS in these models, suggesting DHRSX may not influence the disease pathway as proposed.

We hypothesize that GPAA1, an enzyme responsible for the attachment of glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchors to proteins, contributes to Focal Dermal Hypoplasia (FDH) via defective anchoring of proteins involved in dermal and epidermal development. Specifically, GPAA1 malfunction may lead to improper GPI anchoring of hedgehog-interacting protein (HHIP), crucial for hedgehog signaling pathway regulation, which is vital for skin morphogenesis. Dysfunctional anchoring might decrease HHIP surface expression, impairing hedgehog signaling and leading to the skin and soft tissue abnormalities seen in FDH.

We predict that fibroblasts from FDH patients will show reduced surface HHIP levels compared to controls, with corresponding defects in hedgehog signaling activities (assessed via SMO activation assays). Experimentally correcting GPAA1 function in these cells should restore normal HHIP levels and pathway activity, confirming our hypothesis. Alternatively, unaltered HHIP levels and signaling upon GPAA1 correction would refute the proposed connection.

We hypothesize that galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) deficiency disrupts the metabolic pathway of sex hormone synthesis, contributing to pseudovaginal perineoscrotal hypospadias. GALT deficiency in classic galactosemia leads to the accumulation of toxic metabolites like galactose-1-phosphate, potentially interfering with the synthesis of androgens critical for male genital development. This interference might occur through altered cholesterol biosynthesis or modulation of key enzymes involved in testosterone production. We predict that patients with GALT mutations and hypospadias will exhibit anomalous serum steroid profiles, specifically reduced testosterone or altered testosterone precursors, when compared to controls. Murine models of GALT deficiency should similarly show disrupted sex steroid biosynthesis and hypospadias. Confirmation of this hypothesis requires demonstrating restored testosterone levels and normal genital development in GALT-deficient models supplemented with appropriate sex hormones, whereas persistence of defects would refute the connection between GALT deficiency and disrupted androgen synthesis leading to this specific form of hypospadias.

We hypothesize that NARS1 (asparaginyl-tRNA synthetase 1) dysfunction contributes to Trichothiodystrophy 7, non-photosensitive (TTD7), by impairing protein synthesis fidelity, leading to proteomic instability and compromised epidermal barrier function. NARS1 is responsible for attaching asparagine to its corresponding tRNA during translation. In TTD7, mutations in NARS1 may reduce its efficiency or accuracy, causing amino acid misincorporation or reduced availability of asparagine-bound tRNA. This can result in the misfolding or aggregation of key structural proteins such as keratins and other proteins essential for skin integrity. A specific prediction is that epidermal cells from TTD7 patients will show abnormal keratin aggregation or mislocalization. Experimentally, if overexpressing functional NARS1 in patient-derived keratinocytes rescues normal protein localization and function, the hypothesis would be supported. Conversely, if NARS1 overexpression has no effect, this would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that LARS2 (Leucyl-tRNA synthetase 2, mitochondrial) indirectly affects the progression of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency through the modulation of mitochondrial protein synthesis, impacting ketogenesis. LARS2 is essential for leucine incorporation during mitochondrial protein synthesis, which is critical for maintaining mitochondrial function and energy homeostasis. In the context of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency, reduced ketogenesis exacerbates energy deficiency. We propose that impaired LARS2 activity leads to inefficient mitochondrial protein synthesis, further compromising mitochondrial function and ketone body production from residual lyase activity.

A specific, falsifiable prediction is that reducing LARS2 activity in a cellular model of 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-CoA lyase deficiency will result in decreased mitochondrial protein synthesis and lower ketone body production, compared to controls. Conversely, restoring LARS2 function should normalize these parameters. Confirming this would lend support to LARS2’s role in the disease, while refutation would suggest other compensatory mechanisms.

We hypothesize that NDUFA10, a subunit of mitochondrial complex I, contributes to Alopecia universalis congenita through impaired mitochondrial bioenergetics, affecting hair follicle maintenance. NDUFA10 mutations may lead to reduced NADH dehydrogenase activity, diminishing ATP production and elevating reactive oxygen species (ROS) levels. Hair follicles, highly energy-dependent for growth, may undergo premature senescence or apoptosis from this energetic imbalance and oxidative stress, disrupting normal hair cycling. To test this hypothesis, one could use fibroblasts derived from patients with Alopecia universalis congenita to assess NDUFA10 function. Reduced complex I activity, decreased ATP levels, and elevated ROS in patient fibroblasts compared to controls would confirm the hypothesis. Conversely, normal complex I activity, ATP levels, and ROS comparable to controls would refute it. This link suggests mitochondrial function as a therapeutic target for addressing hair follicle energy deficits in this condition.

We hypothesize that mutations in NDUFS3, a subunit of Complex I in the mitochondrial electron transport chain, disrupt ATP production in chondrocytes, leading to impaired endochondral ossification and contributing to Epiphyseal dysplasia, multiple, 7. NDUFS3 dysfunction decreases NADH oxidation efficiency, reducing ATP and increasing reactive oxygen species (ROS). This energy and redox imbalance hampers the proliferation and differentiation of chondrocytes within growth plates, critical for their development and maintenance. A falsifiable prediction is that chondrocytes from patients with Epiphyseal dysplasia, multiple, 7 will exhibit decreased Complex I activity, reduced ATP levels, and elevated ROS compared to controls. Confirmation would come from observing these mitochondrial dysfunctions and subsequent impaired chondrocyte proliferation in vitro. Conversely, if chondrocytes maintain normal Complex I activity and proliferative capacities despite NDUFS3 mutations, this would refute our hypothesis, suggesting an alternate pathogenic mechanism.

We hypothesize that AK3 (adenylate kinase 3) contributes to familial erythroleukemia through dysregulation of cellular nucleotide homeostasis, leading to aberrant erythroid differentiation. AK3, located in the mitochondrial matrix, facilitates the transfer of phosphate groups among nucleotides, critical for maintaining appropriate ATP/ADP balance. In familial erythroleukemia, mutations or dysregulation of AK3 may lead to altered ATP levels, disrupting energy metabolism and nucleotide synthesis. This imbalance could impair erythroid progenitor proliferation or differentiation, predisposing cells to leukemogenic transformation. 

To test this, we could knock down AK3 expression in normal erythroid progenitor cells and assess for altered ATP/ADP ratios, changes in erythroid differentiation markers, and increased leukemic transformation. Confirmation would be an observed shift towards leukemic phenotypes and disrupted nucleotide levels in AK3-deficient cells. Refutation would be unaltered nucleotide homeostasis and erythroid differentiation despite AK3 knockdown.

We hypothesize that the enzyme TRY-GTA7-1 contributes to the pathogenesis of Focal dermal hypoplasia through dysregulation of the Wnt signaling pathway, leading to aberrant fibroblast activity and dermal malformations. Specifically, TRY-GTA7-1 may aberrantly modify a key Wnt pathway component, altering its interaction with beta-catenin, which subsequently disrupts normal fibroblast differentiation and collagen production. We predict that overexpression or hyperactivity of TRY-GTA7-1 in dermal fibroblasts will result in altered expression of Wnt target genes and reduced collagen deposition, characteristic of Focal dermal hypoplasia. Experimental validation would involve observing an increase in beta-catenin mislocalization and decreased collagen production in fibroblasts exposed to excess TRY-GTA7-1 activity. Conversely, inhibition of TRY-GTA7-1 should restore normal Wnt signaling and collagen deposition. Failure to observe these changes upon modulation of TRY-GTA7-1 activity would refute our hypothesis.

We hypothesize that the enzyme SRD5A3, which is involved in the glycosylation of proteins as part of the dolichol-linked oligosaccharide biosynthesis pathway, contributes to gastric cancer progression by modulating cellular processes dependent on proper protein glycosylation. SRD5A3's role in converting polyprenol to dolichol is crucial for synthesizing glycoproteins that regulate cell adhesion and signaling. Aberrant glycosylation due to SRD5A3 malfunction may lead to altered epithelial cell interactions and enhanced metastatic potential in gastric tissue. A specific, falsifiable prediction is that knockdown of SRD5A3 in gastric cancer cells will result in decreased proliferation and invasion in vitro, due to reduced synthesis of critical glycoproteins, compared to control cells. Conversely, overexpression of SRD5A3 is predicted to enhance these phenotypes. Confirmation would come from observing significant changes in cell behavior and glycoprotein profiles pre- and post-manipulation, whereas absence of such changes would refute the hypothesis.

We hypothesize that SLC27A5, an enzyme primarily responsible for bile acid metabolism, indirectly influences aldosterone production by modulating FXR (farnesoid X receptor) activity in hyperaldosteronism, familial, 1. SLC27A5's dysfunction may lead to imbalanced bile acid levels, resulting in altered FXR stimulation. Understimulated FXR fails to suppress CYP11B2 (aldosterone synthase) expression effectively, causing excess aldosterone production, characteristic of familial hyperaldosteronism type 1. We predict that in a genetically engineered mouse model with SLC27A5 knockout, there will be heightened CYP11B2 expression and plasma aldosterone levels compared to controls. Conversely, restoring SLC27A5 function or directly activating FXR in these mice should normalize aldosterone levels and CYP11B2 expression. Confirmation of this hypothesis would reveal a novel metabolic link between SLC27A5 and aldosterone synthesis, providing a platform for therapeutic intervention. Refutation would occur if SLC27A5 alteration does not impact FXR activity or aldosterone levels in this model.

We hypothesize that ZMPSTE24, an endopeptidase responsible for the post-translational processing of prelamin A to mature lamin A, is mechanistically linked to spastic paraplegia 9A, autosomal dominant, through disrupted nuclear envelope integrity and axonal transport. Mutations in ZMPSTE24 could lead to the accumulation of farnesylated prelamin A, resulting in nuclear envelope abnormalities and dysfunctional axonal transport, crucial in motor neurons. This disruption may cause progressive axonal degeneration characteristic of spastic paraplegia 9A. We predict that in patients with spastic paraplegia 9A, mutant ZMPSTE24 results in increased levels of farnesylated prelamin A and associated nuclear abnormalities in neuronal cells compared to controls. To test this, we would measure prelamin A processing and nuclear morphology in patient-derived neurons. Confirmation would involve detecting elevated prelamin A and altered nuclei, while refutation would involve observing normal prelamin A processing and nuclear structure despite mutant ZMPSTE24 presence.

We hypothesize that the enzyme 15-hydroxyprostaglandin dehydrogenase (HPGD) modulates the activity of the heme biosynthesis pathway via prostaglandin metabolism, influencing the accumulation of porphyrins in Hepatoerythropoietic porphyria (HEP). Specifically, HPGD regulates levels of certain prostaglandins that, when imbalanced, impair heme synthesis and exacerbate porphyrin accumulation in the liver. This occurs through the dysregulation of enzymes such as uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase, crucial in the later stages of the heme biosynthesis pathway. Our hypothesis predicts that HPGD depletion or inhibition will increase abnormal porphyrin accumulation in vitro liver cell models, mimicking the biochemical manifestations of HEP. Conversely, restoring HPGD function should normalize prostaglandin levels and reduce porphyrin accumulation in such models. Confirmation of this hypothesis implies a novel regulatory layer linking prostaglandin metabolism to porphyria, whereas refutation would suggest prostaglandins play a lesser role in HEP pathogenesis.

We hypothesize that adenylate kinase (ADK) directly impacts the pathophysiology of Myasthenic Syndrome, Congenital, 14 by modulating the energy homeostasis at the neuromuscular junction (NMJ). ADK catalyzes the interconversion of ADP to ATP and AMP, crucial for maintaining the ATP levels necessary for acetylcholine release.
